question: What did sugar make of the Atlantic world — an empire of plantations, a slave trade and a new British habit — and what began to turn against it?
summary: This is the sugar century of the British and French Caribbean. Barbados begins the English plantation model with Brazilian know-how in the 1640s and exports 7,000 tons by 1650; Jamaica overtakes it by 1712 with over a thousand mills by 1786; Saint-Domingue becomes the largest producer in the world by 1770 ([[x1]], [[ec1]], [[ec5]], [[ec9]]). The scale is measurable: the slave trade grows from 2,000 Africans a year in the 1570s to 80,000 in the 1790s, and the sugar colonies export more than Brazil by 1700 ([[x2]], [[ec6]]).

Three things travel with the cane. The first is people: enslaved Africans replace indentured Europeans in Barbados in a generation, an English slave code of 1661 removes their rights, and the Zong and the 1791 rising are the two ends of the system's violence ([[l1]], [[o2]], [[l3]], [[c7]]). The second is goods: rum grows into a trade with North America and the African coast, and molasses from the French islands feeds New England's distilleries, which is why sugar law becomes part of the quarrel behind American independence ([[ec4]], [[x3]], [[ec8]], [[o3]]). The third is habit: sugar and tea become the daily food of the British poor, as Eden's budgets and the cookbooks show ([[ec7]], [[l5]], [[e1]], [[e2]], [[x5]]).

By 1800 the same system has produced its critics. Quakers, the Wedgwood medallion and the sugar boycott make slavery visible at the tea table, and the Haitian Revolution ends French dominance, while Marggraf and Achard prove that sugar can come from beet ([[b1]], [[e3]], [[b2]], [[c7]], [[t5]]). The next folio is about what those two events change.

themes.title: Plantation scale: Barbados, Jamaica, Saint-Domingue
text: The folio's economy lane gives the growth in tons, mills and acres, with forests felled and islands taken by war. Each island has its own timing: Barbados first, Jamaica after the 1655 conquest, Saint-Domingue after 1697.

themes.title: Slavery and resistance
text: Africans replace indentured Europeans, the codes harden, mutinies and maroon communities form, and the Zong case shows how slave-ship owners treated the human cargo as insured property. Then the rising of 1791 destroys hundreds of plantations.

themes.title: Rum, molasses and the American quarrel
text: The by-products of sugar make their own trades. Rum goes north and to Africa; New England distills French molasses; parliament's Molasses Act and its successors add to colonial resentment, and the War of Independence threatens the planters' supplies.

themes.title: Sugar and tea at the British table
text: Sugar's share of Britain's imports doubles; refineries multiply in Amsterdam, London and American cities; confectionery and cookery books call for sugar in nearly every recipe; and Hanway and Eden show it reaching the labouring poor.

themes.title: The first turn against it
text: Quaker teaching, the Wedgwood medallion, the English court cases of the 1770s and the boycott of 1791 are the beginnings of the abolition movement; the Berlin chemists show that beet can make sugar.

turning_points.text: Barbados learns sugar from Brazil and begins to export on a large scale.
The English take Jamaica, which overtakes Barbados as the leading British sugar colony by 1712.
Barbados passes the slave code that takes away almost all the rights of enslaved Africans.
Hispaniola is divided at Ryswick; the French colony of Saint-Domingue goes on to be the world's largest sugar exporter.
Marggraf obtains sucrose from beet, though the yield is tiny.
The Zong massacre: the owners claim insurance for Africans thrown overboard.
The rising in Saint-Domingue begins; British abolitionists begin a boycott of slave-grown sugar.
Achard presents beet sugar to the Prussian king; a factory in Silesia follows.

how_to_read: Start with *Economy* for the numbers; open *Lives* and *Order* to see who paid for them, and *Expression* and *Belief* for the new habits and the first criticism. *Exchange* carries the slave trade and rum, and the Nexus links the rise of tea and sugar in Britain to the plantation system.
Several entries record where the sources differ (for example the date of the Sugar Act, or who taught Barbados sugar). Treat those as flags, not as errors in the folio.

The *picture by region* counts the 50 entries: Europe 19, Far East 3, Africa 1, Americas 27; none in Near East, Oceania or Worldwide. The Caribbean dominates, with Europe as consumer, and Asia and Africa at the margins.

sources.intro: A period of abundant secondary literature but still few primary documents read directly; the folio relies heavily on one popular-academic history, with a few general histories as controls.
main: Walvin, *Sugar: The World Corrupted* (about thirty entries), for the British Atlantic, the slave trade and daily life.
Smith, *Sugar: A Global History*, and Buttery, *A Dark History of Sugar*, for the wider story and for some of the numbers.
Mintz, *Sweetness and Power*, for sugar's place in the diet and the Barbadian export figures; Mazumdar for Java and the Dutch in Asia.
contested: Who brought sugar to Barbados: Smith, Walvin and Mintz disagree on the details ([[x1]]).
Palmares' size and the dates of Zumbi's death are repeated from one source ([[c4]]).
The date of the Sugar Act (1760 in Walvin) ([[o3]]).
gaps: Deerr's *History of Sugar* and Eltis's slave-trade database are cited, not read; a source for the Java Cultivation System (after 1830) is still missing.
No French or Portuguese primary or secondary source was used for Saint-Domingue or Brazil in this period.

text: Nineteen entries: the Navigation Acts and the Peace of Paris, Amsterdam’s and London’s refineries, the growth of tea and sugar in English diets from the Complete Confectioner to the farm labourer’s seventeen pounds, Marggraf’s and Achard’s beet, the Zong and the boycott, Wedgwood’s medallion and the tests of slavery in English and Scottish courts ([[o1]], [[c5]], [[ec2]], [[ec7]], [[ec10]], [[x5]], [[e1]], [[e2]], [[t3]], [[t4]], [[l5]], [[t2]], [[t5]], [[l3]], [[b2]], [[e3]], [[o4]], [[o5]], [[x2]]).
Three entries: Dutch Java’s 131 mills, Batavia’s sugar winning Surat from Bengal, and the Qing clearance of the Fujian coast and the taking of Taiwan ([[ec3]], [[x4]], [[w2]]).
One entry: Barbados rum buys enslaved people on the Gold Coast ([[x3]]). The African side of the trade appears through the Atlantic entries elsewhere.

Twenty-seven entries, more than half the folio: Barbados from Ligon to the hurricane of 1675, rum and the slave code, Jamaica’s mills, Saint-Domingue’s rise and revolution, Palmares, Havana, Louisiana and New England’s rum, and the Molasses Act that feeds American resentment ([[t1]], [[ec1]], [[l1]], [[o2]], [[c1]], [[ec4]], [[ec5]], [[ec9]], [[c7]], [[c4]], [[c8]], [[x6]], [[ec8]], [[o3]], [[w3]], [[l4]]).
